claim_ceiling: Direct spatial variation in pollinator assemblage, ungulate damage and trait selection; no randomized A manipulation or demonstrated evolutionary response
decision_note: Gomez et al. 2009: eight populations show spatial turnover in main pollinator functional groups, ungulate damage and floral-trait selection, including divergent selection in some traits.

claim_ceiling: Pollination and herbivory causally alter selection on natural floral traits; this is not a randomized do(A) response and does not satisfy the strict A-manipulated gate
decision_note: Sletvold et al. 2015 factorially manipulated pollination and herbivory and recovered conflicting selection on phenology and reinforcing selection on spur length, but did not manipulate the floral A axis.

claim_ceiling: Landscape simplification alters herbivory-to-display-to-pollination-to-seed-set pathways; local adaptation of resident plants remains an inference and A itself was not randomized
decision_note: Schroeder et al. 2024 studied 14 Finger Lakes sites; herbivory varied with landscape complexity and affected floral display, pollinator contribution and seed set. Pollinator community composition itself did not vary significantly with landscape.

claim_ceiling: Direct multi-audience trait and visitor differences with seed production; no A manipulation, common cue-effect coefficient or evolutionary maintenance test
decision_note: Wang et al. 2022 recovered morph-specific nectar/floral traits, hawkmoth pollination, bumblebee nectar robbing, honeybee pollen feeding and open-pollinated seed production; the trait axis was not manipulated.

claim_ceiling: Pollinators and seed predators both favor yellow flowers in one population; no randomized do(A) and no evidence that opposing selection maintains the color polymorphism
decision_note: Veiga et al. 2015 used path analysis in a Torrestio population and found pollinator- and seed-predator-mediated selection both favored yellow flowering individuals, rejecting an opposing-selection maintenance explanation there.

claim_ceiling: Six-population visitor mosaic and morph-specific reproductive consequences are direct; nectar robbers can also pollinate, so antagonist sign is role-dependent and no A manipulation is present
decision_note: Zhu et al. 2015 quantified visitor assemblages and female fecundity across six Primula secundiflora populations; nectar-robbing bumblebees and syrphids had complementary morph-specific pollination effects.

da Cruz et al. 2026 manipulates ant attendance at post-floral pericarpial nectaries and measures pollinators, herbivores, nectar thieves and fruit fitness, but the manipulated coordinate is post-floral ant attendance/PPNs rather than a floral attraction or display A axis.

claim_ceiling: Direct causal evidence that pollinator-grazer balance drives among-population selection and rapid morph-frequency evolution; existing morph frequency change is not origin of a new private cue or lineage branching
decision_note: Agren et al. 2013: 69 populations on Oland, replicated pollinator/grazer experiments and eight-year grazer exclusion link spatial selection differences to rapid genetic morph-frequency change.

claim_ceiling: Direct component-function differentiation in floral scent supports partial modularity; pollinator preservation on the same manipulated components and evolutionary origin are not identified
decision_note: Kessler et al. 2013 used five transgenic Petunia lines to show that individual scent compounds differ in florivore host-location versus deterrent function; this is direct component modularity mechanism, not a strict linked pollinator-antagonist experiment.

claim_ceiling: Flower color, pollinator communities and selective pressures covary across 12 populations; local adaptation is supported but genetic causality of color differentiation was not demonstrated in this study
decision_note: Sobral et al. 2015/PLOS ONE: across 12 Gentiana lutea populations, flower color affected pollinator visitation, pollinator communities differed with color, and spatial variation in selection explained part of geographic color variation; the paper notes genetic causality of color differences remains to be demonstrated.
